transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it’s a bit of a long story, but I suppose what really brings me in today is this whole situation with the local historical society. I’ve been a member for years, you know, just helping out here and there, mostly with the bake sales and the archives. But recently, they mentioned needing to raise funds for the roof repair on the old schoolhouse, and I just... I don't know, I felt this incredible surge of energy about it. I stood right up in the meeting and basically volunteered to run the entire fundraiser myself. And I mean the *entire* thing. 

I went home that very afternoon and started sketching out these elaborate quilt designs—five different patterns, mind you, all historically accurate to the 1880s—thinking we could auction them off. I was up half the night just looking at fabric swatches and historical records. Then, the next morning, practically at the crack of dawn, I started calling every volunteer on our roster. I was making these incredibly detailed schedules, color-coded and everything, assigning people to shifts for the next three months. I even called the mayor's office to see if we could block off Main Street for a parade, which, in hindsight, was maybe a bit much.

But at the time, it all made perfect sense! I was promising everyone these absolutely impossible deadlines, telling them we’d have the quilts done in a week and the whole town mobilized by Friday. I felt like I could do it all, like I didn't even need to sleep or eat, just work on this project. But now... well, my husband had to practically drag me in here because I’m completely overwhelmed, the living room is covered in fabric scraps and charts, and I haven't actually finished a single quilt block. I just took on so much, so fast, and I couldn't stop myself.
During this time when you were working so intensely on the fundraiser, did you find that you needed less sleep than usual?

Oh, sleep. Well, that’s a whole other story in itself. For a while there—during that first week when the fundraiser idea really took hold of me—I was hardly sleeping at all. I mean, I’d maybe get two, perhaps three hours if I was lucky, and I wouldn't even feel tired! I’d wake up at, oh, maybe 2:30 or 3:00 in the morning, and it wasn't like a groggy waking up. It was like a light switch flipped on in my brain. I’d be lying there in the dark, and suddenly I’d think, "Oh, the flying geese pattern would look so much better with that madder red calico," and I just had to get up right then and there. I’d be down in the living room, cutting fabric or drafting up more of those color-coded schedules before the sun was even thinking about coming up. I’d even have to stop myself from calling the other volunteers at 4:00 AM because, well, I knew *they* were sleeping, even if I felt like I had enough energy to power the whole town grid. 

But now... oh, it’s just completely flipped on its head. Now, I go to bed and I just lie there, staring at the ceiling, worrying about the mess in the living room and all those promises I made to the mayor's office. I toss and turn, and my mind just spins with all the things I haven't done. Or, if I do finally manage to fall asleep, I end up sleeping way past my usual time—sometimes until 10:00 or 11:00 in the morning, which I never do—and I still wake up feeling absolutely exhausted, like I’ve been hit by a truck. It’s just so draining, going from not needing sleep at all to feeling like no amount of sleep is enough.
During that time when you were full of energy and hardly sleeping, did you notice your mood being unusually high, euphoric, or irritable?

Oh, euphoric doesn't even begin to cover it. For those first few days, I felt... well, I felt almost glowing, really. It was this incredible sensation, like every single idea I had was just absolutely wonderful and brilliant. I remember standing in my kitchen, holding up a piece of reproduction indigo bunting, and I just felt this profound sense of joy and purpose, like I was meant to save that old schoolhouse single-handedly and I had all the answers. Everything was just so clear and perfect. 

But... well, you asked about being irritable, and yes, I suppose that was a very big part of it too. Because I had this grand vision, you see, and it made so much sense to me. But if anyone—and I mean anyone, whether it was my husband trying to get me to just sit down and eat a sandwich, or Martha from the historical society asking if five king-sized quilts in a week was actually realistic... oh, I got terribly snappish. I really did. I acted like they were deliberately standing in the way of progress! 

I remember snapping at poor Martha over the phone, telling her that if she couldn't see the vision, she just needed to step aside and let me work because we didn't have time for small-minded thinking. Which is so completely unlike me, I’m usually the peacemaker of the group! I hate conflict. But at the time, I just felt like they were all these little obstacles trying to ruin my wonderful plans, and I simply had no patience for anyone who couldn't keep up with me or dared to question my methods.
Can you tell me if there was a specific period of time when your mood was consistently this high or irritable, or if it came and went in waves during that time?

Oh, it didn't come and go at all. It wasn't like... you know, some people say they have a good day and then a bad day, or they feel energetic in the morning and tired by the afternoon. No, no, it wasn't like that in the slightest. It was just this constant, unrelenting drive. From the exact moment I stood up in that meeting—which was right around the beginning of spring, I remember specifically because the daffodils were just starting to come up near the old schoolhouse steps—it was just full steam ahead. 

I was completely consumed by it, day in and day out, every single minute. That whole overdriven stretch with the historical society project... well, it went on for about five solid months. Five months! Can you imagine? Five months of feeling like my brain was running on rocket fuel, five months of snapping at my poor husband if he even looked at my fabric piles the wrong way, five months of calling the mayor's office and rearranging those color-coded volunteer schedules. 

It never dipped, it never faded into the background. I didn't have a single day where I thought, "Oh, maybe I should just take a break and watch television." I just kept pushing and pushing, riding that exact same wave of energy and irritation, convinced we were right on the verge of this magnificent breakthrough. It was just one long, continuous stretch that went on for those five months until... well, until everything just completely fell apart and the mess got too big and I hit this absolute wall. But before the crash, yes, it was incredibly consistent.
Was there a time when your mood was so high or your energy so intense that it was clearly different from your usual self, and if so, did that period last for at least a week?

Oh, it was definitely different from my usual self. I mean, I'm normally a very steady person, you know? I like things calm. But during that whole five-month stretch, the energy... oh, it was just unbelievable. It was like I had a motor running inside me that wouldn't shut off. 

I remember my husband, Tom—bless his heart, he’s so patient—he would try to get me to just sit down and relax for five minutes in the evening. He’d turn on one of those mystery shows we usually like to watch together, maybe make a pot of tea. But I couldn't do it. I simply could not sit still. We’d be two minutes into the show, and I’d feel this... this pressure building up in my chest, this absolute necessity to be doing something productive. 

I’d jump right up from the sofa—I couldn't even make it to the first commercial break! I’d tell him, "Oh, I just remembered I need to measure the backing for the schoolhouse quilt," or "I have to jot down a new idea for the fundraising flyer." And before he could even say a word, I’d be off, scurrying around the living room, rearranging all my supplies, sorting fabrics by color and era, writing frantic little notes on index cards. It was like sitting still was actually physically painful to me. I just had to keep moving, keep doing, keep organizing. So yes, it was very, very different from how I normally am, and it lasted for that entire time, day after day.
Was there a time when your mood was so high or your energy so intense that it was clearly different from your usual self, and if so, did that period last for at least a week?

Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, yes, absolutely. It was profoundly different from my normal self, and as for lasting a week, oh my goodness, it lasted for those five whole months I was just telling you about! 

But to really paint a picture for you about just how intense that energy was... I know I just touched on the television thing, but it really was the most bizarre experience and it just perfectly captures how wound up I was. Normally, I love to just sink into the sofa after supper. I'm 59 years old, I've earned the right to put my feet up! But during those months, I had so much energy—just this buzzing, electric energy coursing through my veins—that I physically couldn't sit through a single TV show with my husband. Not one! 

Tom would put on one of our favorite British mysteries, and I would try, I really would try to just sit there and watch the screen with him. But my legs would actually start twitching. I just had to jump up. I'd leave him sitting there in the living room because I absolutely had to go measure a yard of floral fabric right that very second, or I'd start frantically writing notes about the historical society's budget on the backs of utility envelopes, or I'd pull out all my storage bins and start completely rearranging my sewing supplies right there on the rug. I would just be buzzing around him while he was trying to watch his program. It wasn't just a fleeting thought, it was this absolute necessity to be active, to be doing, doing, doing. And it went on exactly like that, night after night, week after week, without any break at all.

Was there a specific time during those five months when your mood was consistently high, your energy was extremely intense, and you felt clearly different from your usual self—so much so that other people might have noticed a change in you?

Well, yes, absolutely, people definitely noticed, because... well, the way I felt during that time was just so intense. At the very beginning of it all, I felt... oh, how do I even describe it? I felt almost glowing. Truly! It was this wonderful, radiant feeling, like a light had been switched on inside my head and suddenly every single idea I had was just brilliant. I mean, I would come up with a plan for a new quilt pattern or a way to organize the historical society archives, and it just seemed so obviously wonderful and perfect. I felt like I was finally seeing things clearly and everyone else was just... well, catching up. 

But, you know, the funny thing is, as wonderful as I felt, if anyone—and I mean anyone—tried to question my ideas or even suggest we slow down a bit... oh, I would just turn on a dime. I got incredibly snappish. I remember poor Mrs. Higgins at the society meeting, she just gently asked if maybe we were taking on too much too fast with the fundraiser, and I practically bit her head off! I just felt this intense irritation, this feeling that they were all just standing in my way, deliberately trying to hold me back from doing these amazing things. It was like they were moving in slow motion and I was running at top speed, and I just couldn't tolerate anyone dragging their feet. So yes, my mood was very high, but it had this sharp edge to it if anyone didn't agree with me right away.
After that five-month period of intense energy and high mood, did you experience a period where you felt extremely down, hopeless, or lost interest in things you normally enjoy?

Well, yes... yes, I did. And it was just awful, honestly. It was like someone took that bright, glowing light I was just telling you about and just... snuffed it right out. Completely extinguished it. After all that running around and all those brilliant ideas, I just crashed. And the worst part of it—the part that really upset Tom, and me too, if I'm being honest—was how I felt about my hobbies. 

You see, I have always, always loved checking my garden first thing in the morning. I have these beautiful heirloom tomatoes and a whole bed of dahlias that I've cultivated for years. I would usually be out there at the crack of dawn with my coffee, just enjoying the quiet and pulling a weed or two. And my quilting! Oh, I've entered a quilt in the county fair every year since 1998. I usually spend hours planning the patterns and picking out just the right calico prints. 

But after those five months were over... I just stopped caring. I would sit in the kitchen, and Tom would bring in the mail, and there would be my new seed catalogs and the latest fabric swatches I had ordered, and... nothing. I would just look at them sitting there on the kitchen table and I wouldn't feel a single thing. No excitement, no inspiration, just this heavy, blank nothingness. I didn't even want to open the envelopes. It was like I was looking at someone else's mail. I just couldn't muster up an ounce of interest in the things that used to bring me so much joy, and it just broke my heart, it really did.

After you felt that intense low period following the five-month stretch, did you feel like you eventually came out of it and returned to feeling more like your usual self, or have you been struggling with that depression up until coming in here today?

Oh, doctor, I wish I could tell you that I just snapped out of it and went right back to my garden and my sewing machine, I really do. Tom wishes that too, bless his heart, he's been so incredibly patient with me. But... no. No, I haven't returned to my usual self at all. Not even a little bit. It’s actually the whole reason I’m sitting here talking to you today. 

You see, the thing is, when you're running around like a headless chicken for five months, you make a lot of promises. I had taken on all these custom quilt commissions—people were expecting them for birthdays and anniversaries, and I had promised them these elaborate designs. And then there was the historical society. I told you about snapping at Mrs. Higgins, but honestly, that wasn't the half of it. The volunteer conflicts just completely blew up because I had been so... well, so dictatorial and pushy about the fundraiser. 

And then, when the crash happened and I couldn't even bring myself to open my mail or look at a fabric swatch, let alone sew a straight line, all those quilt orders fell terribly behind. People were calling, leaving voicemails, asking where their things were, and I was just paralyzed. So... ever since those orders fell behind and all the drama with the volunteers blew up in my face, I’ve just been completely stuck. I've been stuck in this awful, low, terribly guilty place for... oh, it has to be about nine months now. Nine whole months of just sitting at that kitchen table, feeling the weight of all the messes I made and just drowning in the guilt of letting everyone down, day in and day out, right up until I finally walked through your door.

During that time when you felt so high and full of energy, did you ever experience any thoughts or sensations that others might find unusual—like hearing voices, seeing things others didn't, or believing you had special powers or abilities?

Well, hearing voices or seeing things, no, nothing like that. I wasn't seeing visions or... or hearing angels, or anything you might see in a movie. But the special abilities part... well, I suppose you could say I felt like I had a special calling, or a special kind of genius, really. It wasn't magic, it was just... clarity. Absolute, undeniable clarity. 

You see, I was working on these heritage quilts. I've always been good at quilting, like I said, I've won ribbons at the county fair, but this was different. I had this vision for a series of quilts that would tell the entire history of our county, going all the way back to the original settlers in the 1800s. And I didn't just think they were good quilts, Doctor. I truly, with every fiber of my being, believed my heritage quilt ideas were going to put our little town on the map. I mean, I thought the Smithsonian might want them eventually! I felt like I had finally found the thing only I could make happen, like I was the only person with the artistic vision and the historical knowledge to pull this off. 

I would sit up until three in the morning, sketching out these incredibly complicated applique designs—corn husks and wagon wheels and the old courthouse—and I just knew, I *knew* that people would come from all over the state, maybe even the whole country, just to see my work. I was already planning the press releases in my head. I thought the mayor would probably give me the key to the city. It sounds so silly now, sitting here in this chair, but at the time, I felt so important. So incredibly important and gifted. I just thought I was destined for greatness, and it was finally my time to shine.

After you started feeling extremely down and losing interest in your usual activities, did you experience any additional symptoms like changes in appetite, trouble concentrating, or thoughts of death or suicide?

Well, my appetite has been just completely gone, honestly. I used to love cooking, especially making these big Sunday dinners for Tom and the grandkids—pot roast, mashed potatoes, the whole nine yards—but lately, just the thought of food makes me feel slightly sick. Tom will make me a sandwich and I'll just stare at it until the bread gets stale. And my concentration... oh, it's just shot. Completely shot. I tried to sit down and read a magazine the other day, just a simple home and garden magazine, and I found myself reading the same paragraph over and over again for twenty minutes without absorbing a single word. It’s like my brain is just wrapped in thick, heavy cotton wool.

And as for... well, as for the other thing you asked about. The thoughts about death. It's... it's hard to talk about, doctor, it really is. I want to be clear, I don't have a plan to hurt myself. I could never do that to Tom, or the girls, I just couldn't. I'm not sitting here figuring out ways to end it all. But... well, I do catch myself thinking, especially when I'm lying awake at three in the morning and all the guilt about the quilt orders and the historical society is just crushing me... I catch myself thinking that it would just be so much easier if I didn't wake up. Just went to sleep and didn't open my eyes again. 

It sounds terrible to say out loud, but it's true. I just think about how peaceful it would be to not have to feel this awful, heavy sadness anymore. And I think... I think about how much easier it would be for everyone else, too. Tom wouldn't have to tip-toe around the house, trying to coax me into eating half a piece of toast. The historical society could just move on and find someone else to run the fundraiser without all the drama I caused. I just... I look at all the mess I've made, all the people I've let down, and I just think, wouldn't it be better if nobody had to deal with my mess anymore? If I was just... gone? It's not that I want to die, exactly, it's just that being alive right now feels so incredibly hard and I just want the burden to be lifted, for me and for everyone I love.
Can you tell me if, during that five-month period of high energy and mood changes, your behavior was so out of character that it caused problems in your relationships or daily responsibilities?

Oh, heavens, yes. "Problems" is probably putting it mildly, Doctor. It completely turned my life upside down, and poor Tom's life too. 

You see, normally I am a very reliable person. Ask anyone in town. If I say I'm going to bring a green bean casserole to the church potluck, I bring it, and I bring it hot. If I have a schedule for cleaning the house, I stick to it. But during those five months... oh, it was like I was a completely different person entirely. I was so caught up in my grand plans, the heritage quilts and dictating every little detail of the fundraiser, that my actual, real-life responsibilities just vanished from my mind. I completely stopped keeping my normal commitments. I mean, the house was an absolute disaster area with fabric scraps everywhere, I wasn't doing the grocery shopping, I was just buzzing around making a terrible mess of things.

And because of how I was acting, and all the bridges I was burning by being so pushy and making all these wild promises I couldn't keep... well, poor Tom has had to take over absolutely everything. All the household routines—he's doing the laundry, he's figuring out what to make for dinner, he's running the vacuum, which he hasn't had to do in our thirty-five years of marriage! He's been an absolute saint about it, but it's just not right. 

And it's not just the house, either. He actually had to be the one to deal with the historical society for me. I had stirred up so much trouble during that time, and promised so many things I never delivered on, that I just... I couldn't face the people who were waiting on me. I couldn't look Mrs. Higgins in the eye after the way I spoke to her, and I couldn't face the women waiting on those quilt orders I abandoned. I was just too ashamed. So Tom had to field all the phone calls, and he had to go down to the society meetings to apologize and try to untangle the massive mess I made. So, yes, it caused a terrible amount of problems. Just terrible. I still can't believe I put my husband through all of that, having to clean up my disasters just because I couldn't face anyone...

Can you recall if there was a specific time when your mood was not only high or irritable but was clearly and consistently different from your usual non-depressed mood, and if so, did that period last for at least one week?

Well, yes, absolutely. It was... it was very different from how I normally am, and it certainly lasted more than a week. It was that whole five-month stretch I was telling you about with the heritage quilts. 

Normally, I'm a very even-keeled person, doctor. People in my quilting circle always say, "Oh, Mary is so steady," you know? But during that time... well, at first, I felt almost glowing. That's the only word for it. Glowing. It was like I had swallowed a sunbeam or something. I would wake up at five in the morning without an alarm clock, and I just felt this incredible surge of joy and energy, like every single idea I had was just wonderful and brilliant. I remember one morning I decided I was going to dye my own fabrics using onion skins and beets from the garden—which I've never done in my life, mind you—and I just thought it was the most magnificent idea anyone had ever had in the history of crafting. I was just practically vibrating with how good I felt.

But... and this is the part I'm not proud of... it didn't stay just happy and glowing. If anyone questioned me, or didn't immediately see my vision... oh, my goodness. I got so snappish. I mean, terribly irritable. I remember Tom just gently asking if maybe I shouldn't be boiling beets at four in the morning, and I completely snapped his head off. I acted like he was standing in the way of progress, like he was trying to stifle my genius. I told him he had no vision and that he was holding me back. And poor Mrs. Higgins at the historical society... she just asked a simple question about the budget for the fundraiser, and I practically yelled at her. I felt like everyone was just moving so slowly, like they were made of molasses, and their questions were just these annoying little gnats getting in the way of my grand plans. It was... it was like a switch had flipped, from feeling on top of the world to feeling furious that the world couldn't keep up with me. And that went on for months, doctor. Months of feeling like that, day in and day out.

Can you confirm that there was a time when your mood was not only high or irritable but was clearly and consistently different from your usual non-depressed mood, and that this period lasted for at least one week?

Well, yes, absolutely, doctor. I know I just touched on this, but it really was... it was a profound shift, and it certainly lasted much longer than a week. It was that whole five-month period with the heritage quilts. 

You see, usually I'm a very steady person. But during that time... well, at first, I felt almost glowing. That's really the only way I can describe it. It was like I had this light inside me, and every single idea I had was just wonderful and brilliant. I was waking up before the sun, full of these grand plans, and I felt like I could accomplish absolutely anything. It was a wonderful feeling, honestly, feeling that capable and that full of joy.

But then... well, it didn't stay just happy and glowing. If anyone questioned me, or if they didn't immediately understand what I was trying to do... oh, I got so snappish. I mean, terribly irritable. If poor Tom or the ladies at the society even asked a simple question, I acted like they were standing in the way of progress. I felt like they were just these obstacles, trying to hold me back from all these important things I needed to do. It was like a switch flipped from feeling on top of the world to just being furious with everyone around me for not keeping up. And that went on for months, day in and day out.
Can you confirm that the time when your mood was high or irritable and clearly different from your usual self lasted for at least 7 consecutive days without breaking?

Oh, heavens, yes. I know we keep circling back to this, doctor, but I can absolutely promise you it was far, far longer than just seven days. It didn't break for a single second. Not for a day, not for an afternoon, not even for an hour! That whole overdriven stretch with the historical society project... I was just going and going like a wind-up toy that someone forgot to stop winding. It went on for about five solid months before everything finally fell apart. 

And when I say it didn't break, I truly mean it. I didn't have a single "normal" Tuesday or a quiet Sunday morning in all that time. Every single day for five months, I was waking up in the dark, buzzing with all those wild ideas about the heritage quilts, snapping at poor Tom if he so much as breathed too loudly while I was working on my plans... It's almost hard to wrap my head around now, looking back, trying to figure out how my body even sustained that level of sheer intensity for nearly half a year. I mean, seven days? If it had only been seven days, maybe I wouldn't have made such a spectacular, embarrassing mess of things with the ladies in town. But no, it was about five months straight of just running completely in overdrive before the bottom dropped out and the whole thing fell apart.

Can you confirm that during that time of high energy and irritability, in addition to it lasting at least seven days, you experienced at least three other symptoms such as inflated self-esteem, decreased need for sleep, more talkative than usual, racing thoughts, being easily distracted, or engaging in multiple activities at once?

Well, yes, absolutely. I know you're asking for three things, and I can certainly tell you about that, because, well, my confidence during that whole time was just... it was completely through the roof, doctor. I mean, usually I'm just Mary, you know? I make my little lap quilts for the nursing home and I help out with the bake sales. But during those five months, I truly believed my heritage quilt ideas were going to put our little town on the map. I was absolutely convinced of it! I thought I had finally found the thing—the one grand, spectacular thing—that only I could make happen. 

I remember sitting at the kitchen table with all these swatches of fabric and historical documents I'd checked out of the library, and I just kept thinking, "This is it. This is my legacy." I honestly felt like I was a visionary, like some sort of master artist that the world was finally going to recognize. I kept telling poor Tom that the state historical society was going to come down and give us an award, that we'd be in all the regional papers, maybe even a magazine! I just felt so incredibly important, like I was the only person who had the brains and the talent to pull off something of this magnitude. It wasn't just a craft project anymore; it was a masterpiece, and I was the genius behind it. So yes, that inflated sense of myself... that was definitely there, big as a house.
During that time when you felt so full of energy and your mood was so high, did you find that you needed significantly less sleep than usual, like only a few hours a night without feeling tired?

Oh, yes, absolutely. I know I mentioned waking up in the dark earlier, but it really was quite extraordinary. For a while there—during those whole five months with the heritage quilts—I was sleeping maybe two, three hours a night at most. And the funny thing is, I didn't feel tired! Not even a little bit. I would wake up at two or three in the morning, and it wasn't like a groggy waking up. It was like a lightbulb switching on. My eyes would pop open, and I was instantly ready to go. I’d be out of bed, pulling out fabric swatches, setting up my sewing machine in the dining room, or drafting these long, detailed letters to the state historical society. I even caught myself almost calling the ladies from the committee at four in the morning once, because I just had to tell them about this new border design I’d thought of. Poor Tom would come out at dawn, rubbing his eyes, and I’d already have been working for hours, just humming along, full of energy. 

But now... well, now it’s a completely different story. Since everything fell apart, my sleep is just a mess. I’ll go to bed and just lie there, staring at the ceiling, my mind just spinning with worry about what people in town think of me now, or I’ll finally manage to fall asleep and end up sleeping until ten or eleven in the morning. And even when I sleep late like that, I wake up feeling like I’ve been run over by a truck. Just completely worn out, like I haven't slept at all. It’s like my body used up ten years' worth of energy in those five months, and now I’m just running on fumes. So yes, during that high time, I hardly needed any sleep at all, but now it’s just the opposite, and neither way feels right.
During that time when you felt so full of energy and your mood was so high, did you notice that your thoughts were racing, or that your mind was jumping quickly from one idea to the next?

Oh, my goodness, yes. Racing almost sounds too calm a word for it, to be perfectly honest with you. It was more like... well, you know how it looks when someone is sitting in front of the television with the remote control, just flipping through the channels as fast as their thumb can push the button? Just flash, flash, flash, and you can't even tell what program is on before it's gone? That was exactly what the inside of my head felt like during those months. 

I would be sitting there at the dining room table, and my mind would just race from the patterns for the quilt blocks—like whether we should use the Ohio Star or the Log Cabin design for the corners, and what colors would look best—and then, before I could even get a pencil to write that down, my brain was already jumping over to the donor lists for the historical society. I’d be frantically trying to remember if Mrs. Higgins had pledged fifty dollars or a hundred, or if we needed to send a formal thank-you note to the hardware store for their contribution. And then, without even taking a breath, my thoughts would completely switch gears again to the church announcements for Sunday, worrying about who was supposed to bring the potato salad for the fellowship hour and if I needed to call the pastor to make sure the quilt project was printed in the morning bulletin. 

It was just quilt blocks to donor lists to church announcements, over and over, spinning so quickly that I couldn't hold one thought long enough to actually finish it! I'd start a sentence to poor Tom about the fabric dye, and halfway through the breath I'd be talking about the church bake sale, and he would just look at me like I was speaking absolute gibberish. I just couldn't slow it down, doctor. It was like I was on a runaway train of my own ideas, and I just had to hold on for dear life while my brain just kept jumping and jumping and jumping. I remember one Tuesday, I had spread out all the files on the floor to try and organize them, but I couldn't even sort one single pile because every time I picked up a paper, my brain was already five miles down the road on a completely different topic!
During that time when you felt so full of energy and your mood was so high, did you find yourself talking more than usual, or feeling like you couldn't stop talking even if you wanted to?

Oh, heavens, yes. Yes, I was talking... well, talking doesn't even really cover it. It was more like a flood, just a constant stream of words coming out of my mouth. I remember, specifically, we had these committee meetings—usually we just meet once a month at the public library, you know, in that little back room near the genealogy section? Well, during those months, I was calling meetings constantly. And when we were in those meetings, I would just take over completely. 

I would stand up there at the front of the table and I would talk so fast... just incredibly fast, rattling off everything all at once. I’d be going on and on about the quilt patterns, and then right into the budgets for the backing and the thread, and then immediately into my plans for the publicity, like how we needed to contact the regional newspapers and maybe even get a spot on the morning news in the city. I had it all mapped out in my head, and I just had to get it all out.

target_item.manifestation: My husband has had to take over household routines and deal with the historical society because I stopped keeping commitments and couldn’t face the people waiting on me.

Oh, heavens, yes. "Problems" is probably putting it mildly, Doctor. It completely turned my life upside down, and poor Tom's life too. 

You see, normally I am a very reliable person. Ask anyone in town. If I say I'm going to bring a green bean casserole to the church potluck, I bring it, and I bring it hot. If I have a schedule for cleaning the house, I stick to it. But during those five months... oh, it was like I was a completely different person entirely. I was so caught up in my grand plans, the heritage quilts and dictating every little detail of the fundraiser, that my actual, real-life responsibilities just vanished from my mind. I completely stopped keeping my normal commitments. I mean, the house was an absolute disaster area with fabric scraps everywhere, I wasn't doing the grocery shopping, I was just buzzing around making a terrible mess of things.

And because of how I was acting, and all the bridges I was burning by being so pushy and making all these wild promises I couldn't keep... well, poor Tom has had to take over absolutely everything. All the household routines—he's doing the laundry, he's figuring out what to make for dinner, he's running the vacuum, which he hasn't had to do in our thirty-five years of marriage! He's been an absolute saint about it, but it's just not right. 

And it's not just the house, either. He actually had to be the one to deal with the historical society for me. I had stirred up so much trouble during that time, and promised so many things I never delivered on, that I just... I couldn't face the people who were waiting on me. I couldn't look Mrs. Higgins in the eye after the way I spoke to her, and I couldn't face the women waiting on those quilt orders I abandoned. I was just too ashamed. So Tom had to field all the phone calls, and he had to go down to the society meetings to apologize and try to untangle the massive mess I made. So, yes, it caused a terrible amount of problems. Just terrible. I still can't believe I put my husband through all of that, having to clean up my disasters just because I couldn't face anyone...

Just flash, flash, flash, and you can't even tell what program is on before it's gone? That was exactly what the inside of my head felt like during those months. 

I would be sitting there at the dining room table, and my mind would just race from the patterns for the quilt blocks—like whether we should use the Ohio Star or the Log Cabin design for the corners, and what colors would look best—and then, before I could even get a pencil to write that down, my brain was already jumping over to the donor lists for the historical society. Oh, heavens, no. No, I wouldn't say I did anything like that at all. I mean, spending sprees? Poor Tom would have an absolute heart attack if I tried something like that! We've been very careful with our budget ever since he retired, and I've always been the one who sits down at the kitchen table every Sunday evening to balance the checkbook to the very penny. Even during those months when I was so incredibly wound up about the heritage project, I never once touched our personal savings. 

I will admit, I was making quite a few trips to the fabric store—probably three or four times a week at one point, because I kept realizing we needed more of this very specific navy blue cotton blend for the sashing between the quilt blocks. But I only ever bought what was strictly necessary, and I always made sure to buy it when it was on sale, keeping every single receipt in a little manila envelope so the committee could reimburse me properly from the project fund. I certainly wasn't going out and buying fancy jewelry or booking flights to Europe or anything crazy like that! 

And reckless driving? Oh, absolutely not. I am a very cautious driver, doctor. I’ve driven the exact same routes around this town for thirty years, and I am terrified of getting a speeding ticket. Even on the days when my mind was just racing a mile a minute and I was absolutely desperate to get to the library for our committee meetings, I still stopped at every single yellow light. I remember one Tuesday afternoon, I was practically vibrating with excitement because I had just had a complete revelation about how to piece together the backing fabric, and I was hurrying down Elm Street, but I still came to a complete stop to let Mrs. Gable's old tabby cat cross the road near the Methodist church. I just couldn't bear the thought of being careless, no matter how fast my brain was going.

As for making big decisions without thinking them through... well, the biggest decisions I was making were entirely about the quilt patterns and the historical society's timeline. I suppose to me, right then in the moment, deciding between a sawtooth border and a scalloped edge felt like a monumental, life-altering choice that had to be made that very second! But it wasn't a real risk, you know? It wasn't like I was signing away our mortgage or quitting a job or doing anything that would actually ruin our lives. So, no, despite all that wild energy and the constant talking and the not sleeping, I wasn't doing anything dangerous. I was still just keeping to my usual rules and routines, I was just... well, I was just doing them all at a hundred miles an hour!
